The ngoni is a traditional string instrument of the Sahel region of West Africa, originating in Mali, Guinea and neighbouring countries. It consists of a wooden soundbox and several strings, and it is finely and elegantly shaped. The ngoni plays an important role in West African folk music, especially as the accompanying instrument for sung narration and storytelling. Its timbre is warm and carrying, between bright and dark, with a distinctive metallic quality and a warm woody ring. In the late twentieth century many West African musicians brought it into modern music production, and it has gained wide recognition on the international stage.

The strings were traditionally of natural fibre, gut or plant fibre, and modern instruments use nylon or metal strings. The posts and neck are made from hard local woods to keep the structure stable. The edge of the soundhole and the decorative parts are often carved in traditional patterns and coloured with natural dyes.

It has come down mainly through traditional West African folk music and as an accompaniment to recited poetry. In the late twentieth century the Malian musician Toumani Diabaté and others brought the ngoni into modern world-music production and made several works fusing traditional and contemporary material, which helped it develop and be recognised on the international stage.
